readingInstruction: Read 2 Kings 11:1-13:25. Athaliah tries to destroy the line of David, and a child king is hidden and crowned. Watch how God preserves the Davidic line, and read the story of Elisha’s death.
settingTheScene: In Judah, Ahaziah is killed by Jehu, and his mother Athaliah, the daughter of Ahab, seizes power by murdering the royal family. The Davidic line seems to be extinguished. In the north, the successors of Jehu rule under Syrian pressure. The section ends with the death of Elisha and a note about God’s covenant faithfulness.
observation: “When Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal family” (11:1).
Jehosheba, Ahaziah’s sister, takes baby Joash and hides him in the house of the LORD for six years (11:2-3).
The priest Jehoiada brings out the king’s son, puts the crown on him, and anoints him, and they shout, “Long live the king!” (11:12).
“Then Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and people, that they should be the LORD’s people” (11:17).
The temple of Baal is torn down (11:18).
“And Jehoash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all his days, because Jehoiada the priest instructed him” (12:2).
Jehoahaz seeks the LORD’s favor, “and the LORD listened to him, for he saw the oppression of Israel” (13:4).
The LORD “was gracious to them and had compassion on them… because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob” (13:23).
interpretation:
Athaliah’s rise is one of the darkest moments for Judah. She kills her own grandchildren to take the throne. The line of David, through which the promised Messiah is to come, is almost wiped out. It looks as though the covenant of 2 Samuel 7 has failed. But a woman named Jehosheba takes one baby, Joash, and hides him in the temple. For six years, while a murderous queen rules in Jerusalem, the hope of the world sleeps in a room in God’s house.

It is a quiet picture of providence. God keeps his promises through the courage of ordinary people, a princess, a priest, a nurse. And in the seventh year, Jehoiada brings Joash out, surrounded by guards, and crowns him. The people clap their hands and shout, “Long live the king!” Athaliah, hearing the noise, cries “Treason!” and is put to death. The covenant is renewed: the king, the people, and the LORD.

Joash begins well. He repairs the temple, collecting money for the work, and the workers deal honestly. But the text says he did right “all his days, because Jehoiada the priest instructed him.” It hints at a faith that depended on his mentor. We learn in 2 Chronicles that after Jehoiada’s death, Joash drifted into idolatry and even killed Jehoiada’s son. Borrowed faith is fragile.

In the north, the picture is grim. Syria oppresses Israel, and the kings continue in Jeroboam’s sin. Yet there is a flash of mercy: Jehoahaz seeks the LORD, and God gives a deliverer. And the last verses of the section give the reason: God has compassion “because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” It is grace that keeps Israel, not merit.

Elisha dies, and even in death his bones bring life: a dead man thrown into his tomb touches the bones and revives. God’s power is not limited by death.
connection: Herod would later try to kill the baby of David’s line (Matthew 2:16), echoing Athaliah. God protected Jesus, as he protected Joash. Jesus is the true king hidden for a time who will be fully revealed. Revelation 12 shows the dragon trying to devour the child. Romans 11:28-29 says God’s calling is irrevocable. The touch of Elisha’s bones points to the resurrection life that flows from Christ (1 Corinthians 15:20).
application:
Think about the quiet acts of faithfulness, like Jehosheba’s, that God uses to keep his promises. Is there one you can do?

Ask whether your faith depends on another person’s influence. How can you make it your own?

Thank God for the covenant that keeps his people, even when they fail.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for hidden acts of courage that preserved his promises.
Ask him to make your faith your own.
Ask him to be gracious to his people.
